description: Kinetic energy, GPE, momentum, stopping distances and why crumple zones save lives.
content_html:
Energy in Moving Objects

Whenever an object moves, it stores energy in its kinetic energy store. The equation is:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$

where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in m/s. Notice that speed is squared — doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy, which is why fast driving is so much more dangerous than slow driving.

Key Fact

Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of speed. Double the speed → four times the kinetic energy. This means braking distance also increases with the square of speed — twice as fast means four times the distance to stop with the same braking force.

Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised above the ground, work is done against gravity and energy is stored as gravitational potential energy (GPE):

$$E_{gpe} = mgh$$

where \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (approximately 10 N/kg near Earth), and \(h\) is height in metres. When the object falls, GPE transfers to kinetic energy (assuming no friction or air resistance).

A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate its speed just before it hits the ground. (Ignore air resistance.)

GPE at top = \(mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100\) J

By conservation of energy: \(E_k = 100\) J

\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 100 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times v^2 = 100 \Rightarrow v^2 = 100 \Rightarrow v = 10\) m/s

Stopping Distances and Road Safety

When a vehicle needs to stop suddenly, the total stopping distance has two components:

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

Thinking distance increases linearly with speed (higher speed → more distance covered in the same reaction time). Factors that increase thinking distance: tiredness, alcohol or drugs, distractions. Braking distance increases with the square of speed (because kinetic energy ∝ v²). Factors that increase braking distance: worn tyres or brakes, wet or icy roads, greater vehicle mass or speed.

Key Fact

Large decelerations during sudden braking generate very large forces on vehicle occupants (\(F = ma\), large negative \(a\) → large \(F\)). These forces can cause serious injury — which is why reducing deceleration time is the key principle behind vehicle safety features.

Momentum

Every moving object has momentum. The equation is:

$$p = mv$$

where \(p\) is momentum in kg m/s, \(m\) is mass in kg, and \(v\) is velocity in m/s. Momentum is a vector — its direction is the same as the velocity.

In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before a collision equals the total momentum after. This is called the conservation of momentum. For two objects colliding: \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2\).

When a vehicle collides, its momentum changes from its speed-before value to zero. This change in momentum is called the impulse:

$$\text{impulse} = F \Delta t = \Delta p$$

A crumple zone is the front or rear section of a car designed to deform (crumple) during a collision. By crumpling, the car takes longer to come to rest — the time over which momentum changes (\(\Delta t\)) increases. Since \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\), a longer time means a smaller force on the passengers for the same momentum change.

This is the precise chain of reasoning you must reproduce in an exam: crumple zone deforms → collision time increases → same momentum change occurs over a longer time → average force on occupants is reduced → injury risk is lower. Saying crumple zones “absorb force” or “act as a barrier” misses the physics and will not earn full marks.

The same principle applies to airbags (increase contact time between driver and steering wheel), seatbelts (stretch slightly to extend stopping time), cycle helmets and padded sports equipment.

Conservation of Momentum: Worked Example

Consider two trolleys: trolley A (2 kg, moving at 3 m/s) collides with stationary trolley B (1 kg) and they stick together. Total momentum before = 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s. After: (2 + 1) x v = 6, so v = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before = 9 J; after = 6 J. The 3 J difference converts to thermal energy and sound, making this an inelastic collision. In a perfectly elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, a distinction the examiner often tests.
exam_tip_html: The crumple zone question is one of the most frequently lost marks in this topic. You must include all steps: the crumple zone extends collision time (\(\Delta t\) increases); for the same change in momentum (\(\Delta p\)), a larger \(\Delta t\) means smaller average force (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)). Simply writing “it absorbs the impact” or “it reduces the force” without the time-extension reasoning earns no marks. For kinetic energy calculations, always substitute before squaring: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\) — a common mistake is to forget the \(\frac{1}{2}\). For momentum conservation, be careful with directions — assign positive/negative signs to velocities moving in opposite directions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) grows with the square of speed — doubling speed quadruples KE and braking distance. GPE = \(mgh\) transfers to KE as an object falls (conservation of energy).
  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Large decelerations cause large forces (\(F = ma\)), which is why sudden stops can injure passengers.
  • Momentum \(p = mv\) is conserved in collisions. Crumple zones extend collision time, reducing the average force on occupants for the same change in momentum (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)).

practice_questions.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of a 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s.
practice_questions.marks:
\(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 1500 \times 400 = 300{,}000\) J (300 kJ)

1 mark for correct substitution into \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).
1 mark for correct answer with unit (J or kJ).

Common error: forgetting the \(\frac{1}{2}\) factor, giving 600,000 J.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using the relationship between force, change in momentum and time, why crumple zones at the front of a car reduce the risk of injury in a collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states crumple zones reduce the force.
Secure: crumple zone deforms during the collision, increasing the time over which momentum changes (\(\Delta t\) increases); since \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\) and momentum change is the same, a greater \(\Delta t\) means a smaller average force on the occupants.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes that this reduces peak deceleration and therefore peak force; links to why the crumple zone design is at the front/rear (passenger compartment is rigid to protect occupants). Correctly rejects the explanation that crumple zones “absorb force.”

[1 mark: crumple zone extends collision time; 1 mark: same \(\Delta p\) over longer \(\Delta t\) means smaller \(F\) using \(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\); 1 mark: therefore force on passengers is reduced → injury risk lower]

practice_questions.text:
A cyclist of mass 75 kg (including bicycle) is travelling at 8 m/s.
(a) Calculate the momentum of the cyclist.
(b) The cyclist brakes to a stop in 4 s. Calculate the average braking force.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(p = mv = 75 \times 8 = 600\) kg m/s [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) Change in momentum \(\Delta p = 600 - 0 = 600\) kg m/s
\(F = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \frac{600}{4} = 150\) N [2 marks: 1 for identifying \(\Delta p\), 1 for correct force with unit]

Alternatively via \(F = ma\): \(a = (0 - 8)/4 = -2\) m/s\(^2\); \(F = 75 \times 2 = 150\) N ✓ [1 mark for either valid method]

practice_questions.text:
A ball of mass 0.5 kg is dropped from a height of 8 m. Calculate:
(a) The gravitational potential energy at the top.
(b) The speed of the ball just before it hits the ground. (Assume no air resistance; g = 10 N/kg.)
practice_questions.marks:
(a) \(E_{gpe} = mgh = 0.5 \times 10 \times 8 = 40\) J [1 mark: correct calculation with unit]

(b) By conservation of energy: \(E_k = 40\) J
\(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 40 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow 0.25v^2 = 40 \Rightarrow v^2 = 160 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{160} \approx 12.6\) m/s [3 marks: 1 for equating GPE to KE, 1 for rearrangement, 1 for correct answer with unit]

practice_questions.text: Explain the factors that affect both the thinking distance and the braking distance of a vehicle, and discuss how Newton's laws of motion have led to improvements in road safety through the design of safety features.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging: lists some factors without explanation.
Developing: identifies thinking distance factors (reaction time, speed, alcohol/drugs/distractions) and braking distance factors (speed, road surface, tyre/brake condition, mass) with brief explanation.
Secure: as Developing, plus explains the physics — braking distance ∝ v² because KE = ½mv²; stopping requires KE to be removed by work done by braking force (W = Fd); larger KE needs more braking distance; also explains crumple zones, seatbelts or airbags using the impulse/momentum principle (\(F = \Delta p / \Delta t\)).
Mastering: as Secure, plus evaluates the trade-off — increasing collision time reduces force but requires the car to crumple (permanent deformation is the cost); risk-benefit framing: society accepts the cost of replacing the crumple zone because the benefit (reduced injury) far outweighs it; links to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis.

[2 marks: thinking distance factors correctly explained; 2 marks: braking distance factors correctly explained with \(v^2\) link; 1 mark: safety feature explained using impulse/momentum; 1 mark: risk-benefit or Newton's law evaluation]

practice_questions.text: A 2000 kg lorry travelling at 15 m/s collides with and attaches to a stationary 500 kg car. Calculate the velocity of the combined vehicles immediately after the collision.
practice_questions.marks:
Use conservation of momentum:
Momentum before = \(m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (2000 \times 15) + (500 \times 0) = 30{,}000\) kg m/s [1 mark]
Momentum after = \((m_1 + m_2)v = 2500v\) [1 mark]
\(2500v = 30{,}000 \Rightarrow v = \frac{30{,}000}{2500} = 12\) m/s [2 marks: 1 for equation, 1 for correct answer with unit]

Common error: not adding masses after attachment, or only using one object's momentum.

knowledge_checks.q: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
What is the correct explanation for why a crumple zone reduces injury in a collision?
options: It absorbs force so the passenger feels nothing
It extends the collision time, reducing the average force for the same momentum change
It reduces the momentum of the vehicle
It acts as a rigid barrier between the passenger and the impact

knowledge_checks.q: Stopping distance equals thinking distance plus _____.
The equation for gravitational potential energy is \(E_{gpe}\) = _____.
Match each safety feature to the physics principle it uses:
right: Deforms to extend collision time and reduce force
Cushions impact and increases stopping time for upper body
Stretches slightly to extend deceleration time and reduce peak force

flashcard_questions.q: What is the equation for kinetic energy, and what do the symbols represent?
flashcard_questions.a: KE = ½mv², where m is mass in kg and v is velocity in m/s.

flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation for gravitational potential energy.
flashcard_questions.a: Egpe = mgh (energy in J, mass in kg, g in N/kg, height in m).

flashcard_questions.q: If a car's speed doubles, what happens to its kinetic energy?
flashcard_questions.a: It quadruples — kinetic energy is proportional to speed squared.

flashcard_questions.q: What is momentum and how is it calculated?
flashcard_questions.a: Momentum (p) = mass × velocity (p = mv), measured in kg m/s.

flashcard_questions.q: State the conservation of momentum principle.
flashcard_questions.a: Total momentum before a collision equals total momentum after, in a closed system.

flashcard_questions.q: Give the equation linking impulse, force and time.
flashcard_questions.a: Impulse = FΔt = Δp (impulse in N s = kg m/s).

flashcard_questions.q: Explain the crumple zone mechanism in one sentence.
flashcard_questions.a: Crumple zones extend collision time, so the same momentum change produces a smaller average force on occupants.

flashcard_questions.q: What two components make up stopping distance?
Name two factors that increase thinking distance.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two: higher speed, tiredness, alcohol or drugs, distractions (e.g. phone).

flashcard_questions.q: Name two factors that increase braking distance.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two: higher speed, wet/icy road, worn brakes or tyres, greater vehicle mass.

glossary_terms.definition: The energy stored in a moving object, equal to half its mass multiplied by the square of its speed.
The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field, equal to mass × gravitational field strength × height.
The total distance travelled by a vehicle from when the driver first sees a hazard to when the vehicle comes to rest.
The distance travelled between a driver seeing a hazard and applying the brakes — depends on reaction time and speed.
The distance travelled from when the brakes are applied until the vehicle stops — increases with the square of speed.
The product of an object's mass and velocity; a vector quantity measured in kg m/s.
The principle that in a closed system, total momentum remains constant — momentum before an event equals momentum after.
The change in momentum of an object, equal to the force multiplied by the time over which the force acts.
A specially designed section of a vehicle that deforms on impact, increasing collision time and reducing the force on occupants.
